# Introduction

In this exercise we will build the **simple linear regression** column of a published table, using the study's own data. We will fit the first few rows together, then you will add two more predictors on your own.

Along the way we will compare our numbers to the paper and find two places in the published table that do not match the data the authors released (a reminder that even published work can be mistake-ridden).

## The study

The study is called "Depression and its determinants among adolescents in Jimma town, Southwest Ethiopia", and was published in PLOS ONE in 2021. A copy of the paper is in `paper/depression_paper.pdf`.

The authors released the survey data they used in the study, which we will use in this exercise. This is available in `data/depression_data.xls`.

## The outcome: the PHQ-9 depression score

The authors looked at different socio-demographic factors that might predict depression among adolescents in a town in Southwest Ethiopia.

The authors measured depression with the **PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)**, a widely used screening tool. It asks how often, over the last two weeks, a person has been bothered by nine problems. For example, one item asks about *"Little interest or pleasure in doing things"* and another about *"Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless."* Each item is rated from 0 ("Not at all") to 3 ("Nearly every day").

![The nine PHQ-9 items and response scale.](paper/phq9_questionnaire.png)

The nine item scores are summed into a total from 0 to 27, where higher means more depressive symptoms. In the data this total is the column we rename to `depression_score`.

## The table we will build

Table 2 of the paper reports, for each explanatory variable, a **simple linear regression** column (one predictor at a time) and a **multiple linear regression** column (all predictors together). We will build only the **simple linear regression** column. 

![Table 2 from Girma et al. (2021). We reproduce the simple linear regression column.](paper/table2_with_values.png)

## Step 2: Run one simple linear regression per predictor

We start with three predictors, one of each type: `chronological_age` (continuous), `sex` (binary), and `grade_level` (polytomous). A simple regression uses **one predictor at a time**. The outcome is always `depression_score`.

The age model is filled in as an example. Fill in the predictors for the other two models.

```{r models}
age_model   <- lm(depression_score ~ chronological_age, data = survey)
sex_model   <- lm(___________ ~ ______, data = __________)
grade_model <- lm(___________ ~ ______, data = __________)
```

Let's look at the sex model with `summary()`.

```{r sex-summary}
summary(sex_model)
```

**Question**: In `summary(sex_model)`, which sex is the reference group? Fill in the blanks in the sentence below to explain the relationship between sex and depression score.

> The reference group is ______. The `sexMale` coefficient is about ______, which means that on average, males score about ______ points ______ (higher / lower) on the PHQ-9 than females.

(Hint: the coefficient keeps its minus sign; the "points ... higher / lower" phrase uses the *size* of that number plus the matching direction word.)

## Step 3: Extract the beta and 95% CI with `broom`

`summary()` is good for reading one model. To build a table we want the numbers in a data frame. `broom::tidy()` does that, and `conf.int = TRUE` adds the 95% CI as columns.

```{r tidy-example}
tidy(sex_model, conf.int = TRUE)
tidy(grade_model, conf.int = TRUE)
```

**Question**: What is the 95% CI for the `sexMale` coefficient? Fill in the blanks in the sentence below to interpret it.

> The 95% CI for the `sexMale` coefficient (the male − female difference) runs from about ______ to ______. Because this interval ______ (includes / excludes) 0, the difference ______ (is / is not) statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

**Question**: The slope estimate for Grade 12 is 1.64. Fill in the blanks in the sentence below to explain the relationship between grade level and depression score.

> Compared with ______ (the reference group), students in Grade 12 score about ______ points ______ (higher / lower) on the PHQ-9, on average.

### Helper for categorical predictors

Now, to turn these regression results into a nice paper-style table, we will create some helper functions.

Most of the formatting code below is fully written out for you. As in the previous table building exercise, we think it's most important to focus on getting the statistics right; formatting can be delegated to a template like this or to an LLM, **as long as you check the values that come out of the fancy code very carefully**.


Below we write one helper function, `cat_rows()`, for categorical predictors.

It will:
- drop the intercept
- strip the variable name off `"sexMale"` to leave `"Male"`
- add back a **reference row** with β = 0

```{r helper-cat}
cat_rows <- function(model, var_name, var_label, ref_label) {
  # non-reference rows: drop the intercept, clean the level label
  non_ref <- tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(level = str_remove(term, var_name)) %>%
    transmute(variable = var_label, level, beta = estimate, low = conf.low, high = conf.high)

  # the reference row: beta is 0 by definition, CI is blank
  ref <- tibble(variable = var_label, level = ref_label, beta = 0, low = NA_real_, high = NA_real_)

  bind_rows(ref, non_ref)
}
```

Run it once on the sex model and compare the result to the raw `tidy()` output above.

```{r helper-cat-demo}
cat_rows(sex_model, var_name = "sex", var_label = "Sex", ref_label = "Female")
```

**Question**: Compared with `tidy(sex_model, conf.int = TRUE)`, name one change that `cat_rows()` made.

Answer: _______

### Helper for continuous predictors

Next, we write one helper function, `cont_rows()`, for continuous predictors.

A continuous predictor has no reference group and just one row, so `cont_rows()` is simpler: it keeps the single slope row and labels it.

```{r helper-cont}
cont_rows <- function(model, var_name, var_label, level_label) {
  tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    filter(term == var_name) %>%
    transmute(variable = var_label, level = level_label, beta = estimate, low = conf.low, high = conf.high)
}
```

```{r helper-cont-demo}
cont_rows(age_model, "chronological_age", "Chronological age", "Per 1-year increase")
```

### Build the first three rows

Now we stack age, sex, and grade into one results frame. Fill in the two blanks for the sex row: the variable name R used inside `lm()`, and the name of the reference group.

```{r combine}
results <- bind_rows(
  cont_rows(age_model, "chronological_age", "Chronological age", "Per 1-year increase"),
  cat_rows(sex_model, "______", "Sex", ref_label = "______"),
  cat_rows(grade_model, "grade_level", "Grade level", ref_label = "Grade 9")
)

results
```

## Step 4: Assemble the table with `gt`

Now, we can assemble the table with `gt`.

Below we write a function, `make_table()`, to assemble the table with `gt`.

We wrap it in a function so we can reuse it after you add your own predictors in Part 2.

```{r make-table-fn}
make_table <- function(results_df) {
  results_df %>%
    mutate(
      `Beta (95% CI)` = if_else(
        is.na(low),
        "Reference",
        paste0(
          format(round(beta, 2), nsmall = 2), " (",
          format(round(low, 2), nsmall = 2), " to ",
          format(round(high, 2), nsmall = 2), ")"
        )
      )
    ) %>%
    select(variable, level, `Beta (95% CI)`) %>%
    gt(groupname_col = "variable", rowname_col = "level") %>%
    tab_header(
      title = "Depression (PHQ-9) score by participant characteristic",
      subtitle = "Simple (bivariable) linear regression"
    ) %>%
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_row_groups()) %>%
    tab_options(table.width = pct(100))
}

```

Now let's call that function on our results.

```{r make-table-call}
make_table(results)
```

## Check these three rows against the paper

Compare your three rows to the paper's simple linear regression column (the Table 2 image near the top).

```{r compare-1}
results %>% filter(!is.na(low)) %>% mutate(across(c(beta, low, high), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

**Question**: Which of these three predictors matches the paper's numbers?

Your answer:

You should find that **sex** matches the paper exactly, but **chronological age** and **grade level** do not. These are the two errors we mentioned at the start.

For age, the data give β = 0.45 (0.18 to 0.71), but the paper prints 0.59 (0.20 to 0.99). For grade, with Grade 9 as the stated reference group, the data give Grade 10 = 1.34 and Grade 12 = 1.64, but the paper prints 0.63 and 0.95. (The paper's table also drops the Grade 11 row altogether, even though those 103 students are in the data and in our model.)

If you find errors in published work, it is sometimes helpful to contact the authors and ask them to correct the table. For now, we ignore the errors and continue with the exercise.

# PART 3: One framework for t-tests, ANOVA, and continuous predictors

Last week you compared group means with a **t-test** (two groups) and **ANOVA** (three or more groups). This part shows that simple linear regression answers the same questions for categorical predictors, while also handling continuous predictors that those tests cannot handle.

## A binary predictor: regression and the t-test

A two-sample t-test also compares the two group means. It asks whether the difference between them could plausibly be zero. Under equal variances, that test and the regression slope test are the same calculation.

Run both below and compare the output.

```{r ttest-vs-reg}
t.test(depression_score ~ sex, data = survey, var.equal = TRUE)
tidy(sex_model)
```

**Question**: Compare the p-value from `t.test()` with the p-value for `sexMale` in `tidy(sex_model)`. What do you notice? (The t statistics may differ in sign depending on which group is subtracted from which; the p-values should match.)

Your answer:

**Question**: The `sexMale` estimate in `tidy(sex_model)` is the difference in mean depression score between males and females. Run the code below to compute those two group means yourself, then subtract female from male. Does your hand calculation match the regression coefficient (up to rounding)?

```{r check-means}
survey %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(mean_dep = mean(depression_score))
```

Your answer:

## A polytomous predictor: regression and ANOVA

With more than two groups, there is no single slope. Instead, `lm()` creates one coefficient per non-reference level (Grade 10, Grade 11, Grade 12), each comparing that grade to Grade 9.

A one-way ANOVA does not report those individual comparisons. It asks one **overall** question: is there any difference among the group means? That overall test can be accessed in the regression framework too. Scroll to the bottom of `summary(grade_model)` for the model's F statistic and p-value, which test whether the set of grade coefficients are all zero together.

Run both below.

```{r anova-vs-reg}
summary(aov(depression_score ~ grade_level, data = survey))
summary(grade_model)
```

**Question**: Compare the p-value from the ANOVA with the p-value at the bottom of `summary(grade_model)`. What do you notice?

Your answer:

## Continuous predictors

The t-test and ANOVA both compare group means, so they only work with categorical predictors. To use a t test or ANOVA with a continuous variable like age or social support, you would first have to cut it into groups, throwing away information in the process.

Regression has no such limit. You already saw this with `chronological_age` in Part 1: a continuous predictor goes into the same `lm()` call and comes out as a single slope, the change in mean depression score per one-unit increase in the predictor.


# Optional ungraded challenge: ask an LLM for a figure-table

This is optional and ungraded. The goal is to practice using an LLM for **presentation code**, while still checking the statistical values yourself.

The published table is clear, but some papers combine tables and graphics in one figure. For example, look at Fig 2 in this PLOS ONE paper: <https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0304487>

Your challenge: use your LLM to turn your existing `results_full` table into a figure-table with:

- a left panel with the variable and level labels
- a column showing the beta and 95% CI as text
- a forest plot showing the simple-regression slopes and 95% confidence intervals
- stars beside rows where the 95% CI excludes 0

Use `results_full`, which you already created. 

Here is an example prompt. Be sure to include a screenshot or download of the example figure style in your prompt.

> Consider the R Data frame below :

> [PASTE YOUR resultsDATA FRAME HERE]

> I have attached a screenshot of the example figure style I want. With a forest plot of the coefficients and 95% CIs. Give me code to build it. 

> The authors shared this script that shows how to build such a table: <https://github.com/kendavidn/yaounde_serocovpop_shared/blob/v1.0.0/scripts/infection_regn_2.R>

When you get code back, check at least three values against `results_full`: one reference row, one categorical coefficient, and one continuous coefficient. Do not trust the plot until those values match.
